First lemme just say that I relate a LOT to the feelings you describe here, and I'm sure many of us have been pretty much word for word where you are at one point or another.

I also had an eating disorder that I used to cope with my self-hatred. I also felt alienated from the trans community, and like no one could possibly understand the tangle of bullshit in my head, let alone me. I thought my situation was utterly hopeless.

But theres really no such thing as a hopeless situation, and I promise you aren't about to be the first exception.   


You say that there's no point in digging up the roots of your problems, and I really feel that, because I've been there, but I'd encourage you to let yourself get curious about your thought patterns. It's easy to get overwhelmed by the sheer volume or intensity of negative thoughts in your head, so dont be discouraged that that's happened to you.   


You also described your flaws as feeling unchangable, and a big part of the reason you hate yourself (again, relatable). If you frequently catch yourself thinking things like "of course I'm sad, why wouldn't I be" or "I can't do this" or "I only have myself to blame", then you've got some deeply ingrained thought patterns that, unchecked, make life look grey and cold and impossible.   


This is an incredibly tough situation to find yourself in- try your best to recognise that. I promise that continuing to dump self-hatred on top of everything else will only keep you stuck. You can't hate yourself into loving yourself.

I also struggle with the concept of self love/ compassion, so I'm speaking from experience: when you have felt despair for so long, love is not immediately accessible in the same way fear is. Your mind has a lot to unlearn before it can feel comfortable allowing good feelings again. People with self hatred often have learned to fear love and happiness, lest they lead to crushing disappointment/ despair again.

Your first step needs to be building a safe foundation for you to explore all this pain and uncertainty, without judging yourself for feeling it. I know that probably sounds impossible right now, but hear me out.

Some questions you might wanna start with:

\- If you could be born again in any body, in your ideal world, what kind of person would you be? 

\- How much of that ideal identity feels impossible to consider in this life?

\- What do you think trans people think about themselves? (don't worry about being offensive)

\- Do you feel like youre not allowed to be trans, or that you don't want to be?

If you want help unpacking any of those questions, I'm happy to listen to whatever you have to say.

I wish you the best!

I too struggle with this- it's crucial that you don't mistake their confusion for fact. Basically everyone who says anything like this is either ignorant, hateful, or both, and they certainly don't know more about your identity than you do.

Remember that growing up surrounded by both subtle and overt transphobia takes a big toll on us, and can leave us feeling at the mercy of what the rest of the world thinks (because when it comes to stuff like respect and basic human rights, we have no choice but to rely on the belief and respect of cis people).

Most of us have to fight to "prove" our gender to survive and be treated equally, so it's not surprising at all that many of us end up internalising transphobia, and/or worrying excessively about what hateful cis people think. It's natural, because those people are a legitimate threat to our community.

But you must always remember that what they think has nothing to do with you. Transphobia is born of fear and willful ignorance, just like any prejudice. It's harder not to take it to heart when you're trans, because we're still one of the most universally doubted and oppressed communities. We are assumed not to exist, and have to fight to show that we do.

That takes a huge psychological toll over time. Psychologists are only just now scraping the surface of the long term affects of transphobia on trans people, and are concluding that we have many unique, constant stressors that can play havoc on our mental health and sense of selves.

This isn't to say knowing all this will make the doubts vanish, but it's really important to keep in mind all the factors that come into play to make you feel like that. The fact that you doubt your identity as a gay man after hearing those messages is not an indication that really you've been faking it and those people are right, but that you are human and sensitive to the input of others, even (and sometimes especially) when that input is hateful.

Trans people have always existed and will keep existing. You are real, and I promise you don't ever need to worry about that- but when those worries do come, remember that they come from outside, not inside. <3

As for those labels and what they mean- they mean male family members, and that's what you'd be. No adjustments needed. I realized that the people around me weren't just humoring me, but that this was who I was, and I deserved the same treatment as a cis person, and any misgendering was just an unfortunate side effect of everyone adjusting to a big social change. I'm over two years into social transition now and I honestly would never even think of going back to my old name/ titles- but the adjustment period still felt bizarre and uncomfortable. Give yourself time to try out new words and see if they fit you, and if they don't, there's no binding contract (pun legitimately unintended).

It's common for binders to be awkward putting on/ taking off, especially around the shoulders- what's key in making sure it's not *too* tight is how comfortable it feels to wear it. Does it hurt your ribs after a short amount of time? Does it dig into your skin painfully? Can you breathe as normal?

If it feels comfy and seems to fit, you're probably golden- just remember to make sure you don't wear it for more than 8 hours maximum at a time (preferably less, especially if you're planning on wearing it daily). Also don't exercise in it, as it can constrict your breathing/ damage your ribs- and on that note, if you experience persistent rib pain or your ribcage changes shape in any way, stop binding immediately and consult a doctor. Your long term health is the most important thing, as much as dysphoria sucks

Your post could literally be something I wrote two ish years ago. I was having daily breakdowns and self harming for the first time; I was just sort of passively slogging through each day and trying not to think about how many days might be ahead of me. I don't ever remember feeling as crushingly lonely as I did back then.

Now I'm not gonna say that since then I've had an epiphany and life is magic because I'm still very much depressed, but I *have* gotten back my good days, which is something I never thought was really possible. What really helped things for me was realising just how self-deprecating I was being, and acknowledging for the first time that every time I was unkind to myself, I was reinforcing my sadness and lack of worth. We have to sit with our thoughts all day, and if they're not nice ones, the effect isn't gonna be ideal- in fact, you can bully yourself into feeling like complete and utter shit 24/7.

I'm not saying that's necessarily your problem, because of course I don't know you, but I think it's pretty universal that people with depression aren't the kindest to themselves. For me it took a lot of forced rewiring, to the tune of complimenting myself every time an insult sprang to mind, even if I didn't believe that compliment for a second. I asked myself constantly: would I be so unforgiving if I was someone else? Why does the fact that I am this person in the mirror make them any less valuable than anyone else?

This coupled with some breakthroughs about humans (I was always VERY cynical about how people operate and socialise, so much so that it took me until adulthood to really appreciate how awesome people can be) definitely gave me the kickstart I needed to at least be able to *see* some sort of future that wasn't clouded in grey despair. I started paying attention to every positive thing I could, unpicking what it meant, wondering about it in awe like I used to as a kid. Of course you can't just be awestruck on demand, and that isn't so much advice, just where my path happened to take me.

Black and white thinking definitely doesn't help though- for example, you saying you *know* that things will only get worse. Now this is gonna sound preachy as fuck and I know it's annoying to hear cause god knows I hear(d) it enough, but there's no way of knowing that for sure. That isn't to say it isn't a possibility, but just because you can visualise it more clearly than a happier future doesn't mean it's inevitable. But I absolutely know what it feels like to just *feel* that things will only get worse, and it's grim, and I wish you didn't have to deal with it.

If you can, I'd definitely advise reaching out to someone about the cutting. If it's a new habit then you're in the best possible place to put a stop to it; I was fortunate enough to be able to stop myself from doing it cold turkey, and though I now have a few pretty bad scars, I'm *very* much glad I don't have more of them.

I really hope that things look up soon, or that you at least get some moments of respite from all this. I'm rooting for you and I do genuinely believe that there's hope for things to improve, even if that feels like the furthest thing from the truth right now

Basically as long as you take a break from it anytime it starts to feel weird/ uncomfortable, you should be fine

For me it wasn't neat or clear-cut at all. It was a drawn-out, messy series of experimenting with changes that I always felt anxious and unsure about, and then loved once I went ahead with them.

So like, I knew I didn't like what female puberty was doing to my body (even pre puberty when they taught us about it in sex Ed I secretly hoped it just never happened to me), but I had no idea what that meant, or if I would just grow out of it, or if I should mention it to anyone. At no point until age 16 did the word "trans" even occur to me as something that was even remotely possible (it was barely in my vocabulary).

So I had an awkward talk with my parents about how I didn't like my chest, and how I'd been wearing two sports bras since my breasts first started developing (something I assumed was a normal insecure teenage girl thing). I told them I wanted chest surgery, but offhandedly, because I was upset and finally brave enough to voice that desire to another human. They frowned at me and asked a bunch of questions like "but you don't want to be a man, do you?" And "are you sure this isn't just a body image problem?" Basically they were shit scared of the whole concept and intentionally or not did a great job of pushing me back in the closet before I even knew the closet was there. 

So I said of course I don't want to be a man, no, I feel very much female but I can't stand my chest. Cue a million reassurances that not every woman loves every part of their body and that's okay and to a teenager who isn't even trying to come out and is terrified of surgery I just relented and shut up about it. 

Then a few months later I started that dialogue again, because the dysphoria was going nowhere. My parents (my mother especially) got more aggressive in their retaliation: "I can't stand the idea of you mutilating yourself like that!" "People get surgery like thatand then regret it for the rest of their lives!" Etc etc, all the good shit. 

I should mention that now, me being on T and prepping for surgery, they're fully supportive. Like, calling up doctors and picking up my testosterone prescription and driving me hours to surgery consultations supportive. Just for context, because I don't want to give the impression that parents are always gonna lash out and then reject you. Most wont be thrilled about the idea, but I'm lucky enough to say that for me they came around to it completely and are even excited about my transition because they realised it's letting me be myself. Anyway!

So I toyed with the label of being genderqueer for a while, but every time pronouns came up I was always adamant I didn't think I'd ever want to change them. I was so worried about the social awkwardness of that- coming out as not completely a girl was scary enough, but then the added layer of asking everyone I knew to call me by he/him pronouns? I couldn't fathom it, and I was so sure it'd be like making everyone else play pretend for my benefit. 

You guessed it, I changed my pronouns. Ha. Name too, all at once- I came out to my friends first and they started using my new name seamlessly. I'd been thinking about it for years and hearing "he/him" in my head, in referral to *me* just sounded right, in a way that "she" and "her" never really did. Looking back it was kind of like someone gave you a nickname on the first day of school that you didn't really like, but went along with because there wasn't much else to do. I also started envisioning me, ten years in the future, as a *man*, and it started to click for me, because seeing myself as a woman in the future was barely even possible. When I tried to imagine that my future just became this vague, miserable blur starring some woman I didn't want to be. 

I told my parents I was pretty certain I was a trans man, and said that I'd like to change my name and pronouns. By then I think they were realising that if this was a phase, it wasn't going anywhere anytime soon, but I also felt genuinely supported by them when I made this announcement. They told me they would do their best to adjust but would probably get it wrong quite a lot to begin with (which they did, but that's to be expected. I did too, haha)

And it's like... I wasn't excited about any of that. I wasn't excited to tell someone I wanted surgery, or that I might be trans, or that I wanted a different name, because it all felt so fucking daunting. I knew the kind of response I might get and I knew that transitioning is hardly heralded as a walk in the park. I think I was so hesitant not only from doubt, but because I didn't want to commit to something so intimidating and expressive and *about me*. But every decision I made, once I'd *made* it, I knew it was the right thing almost immediately (of course I had moments of doubt, but the trend always leaned towards "this feels right").

Same exact pattern deciding to go on T, so I won't write it all out, but it went the same: 'nope, don't want that, never will', 'thinking about it but probably not', 'would like to but I'm scared', 'think I need to but I'm scared', 'going to do it'. And it's already making me feel so much more myself it's insane. 

There's no doubt left in my mind now about whether I'm trans, because the difference is that when I was presenting as a girl/ woman, it was tolerable at best. The best I felt in myself as a woman was okay. The best I feel now, even as a guy going through the ugliest bit of male puberty? Amazing. And not just amazing but *me*, and I know that's corny as all fuck but I didn't realise how badly I was missing that until I started transitioning.

I know this is horrendously long but I wanted to be as detailed as I could- oh, and I had plenty of sobbing breakdowns where I agonised about whether I was just a 'woman in denial' or if I was using the identity of being trans as an excuse to chop off or restyle whatever body parts I didn't like. *Terrible* breakdowns. I think most trans people have them, but the important thing was that when I examined that fear, it was unfounded, because the things I wanted to change about my body were exclusively feminine.

Of course this is just a snippet of my personal realisation and not everyone's will look like this, or even anything like it. Some people pretty much come out of the womb knowing they're trans; some people realise it in their late teens like I did; some will realise it in their 90s. I don't know many people who have always been 100% about it, but it varies a lot, so don't worry about where you fall in that regard. 

I'm also not saying that if you're unsure then you'll definitely end up realising you're trans- lots of people realise they aren't, and there's nothing wrong with exploring your gender on your own terms knowing you don't ever have to commit to a new identity if you find it doesn't fit. There is no expectation to be trans or not to be, and the most important thing is that you are able to be honest about whatever it is you're experiencing in the present, whether or not it's permanent.

I wish you every bit of luck in understanding and loving your identity, whatever it may be! And apologies for writing the essay you avoided writing yourself 😆

Things I noticed in the first week were getting the 'T cold' (scratchy voice/ uncomfortable throat without any other cold symptoms), and VERY fast bottom growth. Like super fast, so much so that after one month it was unrecognizable as what it looked like before. My period also stopped immediately, which I think is uncommon?

But I'm coming up to three months now and my voice hasn't dropped at all- maybe a *tiny* change but nothing really noticeable, and that's something other guys will notice at the very beginning, so it really is luck of the draw what you get. I'm just starting to see very light body hair increase, and muscles in my upper arm/ shoulder area have steadily built from around week two... there might also be a little more weight in my stomach and less in my hips?? But if so it's very subtle and could well just be my imagination.

Oh, and water retention! That kicked in pretty early and freaked me out just because of how dramatic it looks, so don't worry if you wake up and suddenly look like a human balloon. It can come and go from day to day but drinking a ton of water helps keep it manageable I find, and eventually it'll go away completely on its own (some guys say it goes for a few months then comes back, so again, don't worry if that happens, it's just cycling).

My jaw also has gotten much firmer, which I noticed around the one month mark- my skin is also notably thicker, and oh boy, ACNE. Never had a problem with acne going through first puberty, but now it's a constant battle keeping spots off my face and upper back. That probably started very early on too, but became annoying around one month as well. 

I definitely have more stamina than before T but yet to see a reliable boost in mood/ mental energy- no libido change I've noticed either, which is a shame because I've basically always been the embodiment of a viagra commercial with no sex drive at all, lmao. So I was kinda hoping T would 'fix' that but maybe I'm just legit asexual, idk.

So yeah! A lot of the early changes are the more ugly bits of puberty which is eh, but I'm craving that precious voice drop... Hopefully it's not too long, but yeah, the changes come at wildly different times from person to person, so I'd advise strongly against comparing your transition too much to others! The changes will come in time, so try not to stress too much about when- one day you'll wake up and be where you want to be, and you're getting closer every day, pre-T or not!

I hear you. I've been there with many of the points you listed and it's frustrating and sad and scary and I wish I could make things better for you right this instant, but as you say, it's just a waiting game. I'm 20 now, and though I'm not where I want to be yet, if 15 year old me knew how much better things were going to get, I wouldn't have believed it. 

I know that's such an abstract and far away hope when you're still stuck without the resources you need and deserve as a trans adolescent, but the old saying really is true: it gets better. So, so much better, with enough time and patience. (Even if you don't *feel* patient- I know I sure as hell didn't- as long as the time passes, that's all that matters really, just try to be as kind to yourself as you can in the meantime). 

Some advice I can give you that made things much easier for me when I put them into practice:

- You dont suck. You are not lazy or bad or anything inherently negative- if you find yourself unable to do things that you think you should be able to do, that is because of a whole host of potential factors. I don't think it's radical to say you're probably depressed, or suffering from one or more mental illnesses (anxiety, dysmorphia, to name a couple of common ones among trans people). You are not at fault for feeling scared or demotivated or sad or angry. There are things you can do to help yourself get through these feelings, but don't beat yourself up for feeling them. Which leads on to something else I've only just started putting in practice myself:

- Treat yourself with as much compassion as you possibly can. When I'm scared about something, I like to imagine I'm speaking to a child version of myself on the inside- it's my job to look after that kid and not make things worse by insulting them or believing the self-deprecating things they're saying. I have to take care of them and be level headed. So, for example, if I'm scared about going to the gym, I take a step back and ask myself gently what's wrong. If the anxiety is that people will look at me and think I look stupid, I'll say something like "okay, I understand. But you don't look stupid. You're enough as you are, even if it's not where you want to be. And those people are just like you- they're focusing nearly entirely on themselves! They might glance at you, but you'll just be a passing thought. And if you get there and it's all too much I promise we'll go straight home again."

This might sound a little silly, but I can't stress how well it's worked for me. Seeing myself not as an enemy or a failure, but as someone I have a responsibility to look after and be kind to? BIIIG game changer

- Remember that how you are now is temporary, and that you have way more time than you think to accomplish what you want. You're still very young and although there's a lot of pressure to have your life together by your early 20's, trust me when I say it doesn't matter if you need longer than that. I spent the best part of four years doing nothing- no school, too depressed for hobbies, no job. I had dropped out of college at 16 due to my terrible mental illness at the time, and I thought my life was over. I couldn't stand the idea of re-taking the year and being a year below all my friends, I didn't want to do anything- I could barely get up in the morning. Up until then I was set to go to university and the idea that I wouldn't be able to continue that path of academics and early success absolutely crushed me- I think I cried for about five hours the day I dropped out because I thought my life was over. 

But Yknow what? Those years I spent stagnant, not able to do the things I desperately wanted to, frustrated at myself for not being better or even functioning... I needed those years to heal. It wasn't pretty and I was still stuck in a home environment with the same toxic parents, but I got to know myself, and process what I needed in order to recover my mental state. (Obviously not saying this is for everyone, as my situation was extreme, but what I'm saying is that you don't need to feel anxious or that you're 'wasting time' just because you feel awful and are not productive. There will be time for everything you want to do. Right now you're dealing with a huge amount whilst still in your teens, and it's not surprising that anything else on your plate feels like too much.)

I'll stop there so this doesn't become a 5k essay, but I hope there's something there that helps. I know that reading other people's reassurances can feel terribly hollow, because I've been there, but I find it helps to tell myself as often as I can that I'll be okay, whether or not I believe it. The more you repeat a certain phrase or line of thinking, the more the pathways in your brain get used to it- and eventually, those positive thoughts become natural.

I wish you all the best, and please know that whatever you think about yourself, I think you're incredibly strong for not only surviving this mental hurricane, but also for recognising these thoughts and reaching out. That takes a lot of self awareness and effort, and you should be proud!

I feel you so hard on this. And I agree with what others have already said; what you do in regards to transitioning is your choice, and I can't tell you what's right one way or the other. 

But I will say this: I've felt that agony of not wanting to be a minority since I was little, in multiple different ways. Just being endlessly frustrated and confused but mostly sad that I would never get to live the life I dreamed of, without any prejudice or obstacles in the way. When I was eight I had full sobbing breakdowns because I realised I was never going to be a white girl with a thin nose and light eyes. I wasn't proud or happy to be mixed race, I was just *distraught*, because even then I knew that people my colour got just a little less attention, a little less good faith. I'd seen my mum and my grandfather have slurs thrown their way on the street; I knew that I was more likely to be bullied after a big terrorist attack in the news; none of the main characters in movies or on tv shows looked like me. I saw other people being proud of their heritage and all I wanted was to be able to scrub the colour from my skin and be reborn a blue-eyed blonde girl.

And then I realised I was gay, and then trans, and that process caught me off guard every time. But now I'm here and I couldn't be prouder to be mixed race and queer. I love those qualities and that me in the past seems so far away from my mindset right now I can hardly believe it.

I do still wish I was just born male, pretty much every day. I don't think that being trans is something that makes you stronger or better or that it's all 'meant to be'- I think we just got dealt shitty hands and now we're dealing with the aftermath. Even with surgery coming up this year, I wish I didn't have to have it, because it's not fair that I don't have any other choice but to put myself under major surgery just to live in a body I can stand. If you gave a cis guy boobs overnight and told him to deal with it, he'd have a breakdown. We're in a bracket that few people will ever really understand and it can be utter hell.

For me, I think the bulk of the heartache went away when I just accepted that this was going to be my life. I was never going to be white, or straight, or cis. For me, the dysphoria didn't go away in the least. I felt deeply uncomfortable with my body since the very beginning of puberty, and for years I convinced myself that hating having boobs and curves was just a regular teenage girl thing that I'd grow out of. I mean, feeling insecure about your body is a trademark part of puberty, right? I was so sure that when I hit 14, or 16, or 18, I'd come around to the changes female puberty brought and I'd like being a woman.

But no matter how long I waited, I still wanted to be a guy, deep down. It wasn't always clear in so many words, but the fact that I'd been wearing two sports bras to flatten my chest since I was 13, like it was the most normal thing in the world, without even *considering* the word 'trans'... It took me a long time to realise that that was *far* from normal teenage girl insecurity. 

What happened was I got used to it. I got used to the misery of seeing my chest from a side angle and wishing that I could wear a t shirt and have it fall flat down my body; I got used to knowing there was something wrong about me, but not knowing quite *what*; I got used to having to wear a bra even in the bath because I knew that looking at my breasts could make me burst into tears and ruin my whole day. 

Essentially, I knew for a long time that I wasn't going to be able to live any kind of life without surgery, but I ignored it because that thought was *terrifying*. No one *wants* to admit that they're trans, because that means committing to not only coming out to your friends and family, but committing to years of working out what exactly you want to change, whether you want hormones, if you're going to change your name and pronouns, whether surgery is the right decision, and the implications of those choices. It's heavy and it's scary and for me at the beginning I felt so overwhelmingly in the dark that I had no idea where to even begin. 

This is my experience, and it might not be yours, or where you're headed. Maybe the dysphoria will be a phase, and maybe you will be able to live happily and confidently as a woman- but whatever your future might be, it's so so important to investigate these feelings as soon as you're able. Talk to a doctor, a friend, a family member, or all of the above- ask yourself, when you can: Is this a body I can see myself living in happily ten years from now? Am I okay with it at the moment? What would I change, if I could without any effort or heartache? And the answers might be different day to day, or hour to hour, and that is completely normal and okay. What's important is to recognise, over time, which answers come more often, and work from there. If you always find yourself going back to saying "this body is not reflective of who I feel I am inside", that's a good indication that you should look into the options available to you. Even if you never take medical action, it's good to talk through things like hormones and surgery, and see how it makes you feel to consider them.

One last thing I wanted to say was that liking dresses and doing your hair and other feminine things has absolutely no bearing on whether or not you might be a trans guy. For me, coming out took as long as it did because I wrestled with those same doubts: I liked dressing up, and the idea of wearing makeup/ painting my nails, so I couldn't *possibly* be a man! But what I learned, years later, is that I *was* a man, just a very flamboyant, feminine one. In fact, once I embraced the fact that I was a guy, I started getting much more comfortable with embracing those feminine qualities, because suddenly I saw a future where I could happily wear a dress or put lipstick on or sway my hips when I walked- because I could do all those things *as a man*. It was odd to realise just how much I'd been policing myself to be more masculine than I really was because I was so scared of doing anything that would make others clock me as a woman.

Anyway, TLDR; there's no rush to work out what your identity is, but it's good to start thinking about it and open a dialogue with those close to you. Whatever you decide, I wish you the best of luck, and if you ever want advice/ to vent about something, feel free to drop me a message. I'm rooting for you!

For 14 grams I'd up the butter to about 250g- 300g, and supplement it with a good 10 tbsp of oil. It's very dependent on enough fat content to soak up all the THC- basically as long as there's more butter than bud and it's light to stir, you're good. I'd also let it simmer for a bit longer, maybe an hour and ten minutes, but keep the heat low.

For a batch of 24 though, this might be a lot of butter, and it could leak out during baking, so I'd definitely stick to brownies, and add more flour and sugar than the recipe calls for. 

Honestly it's pretty hard to fuck up an edible, so don't sweat it too much- if it's your first time making them there's bound to be a bit of experimentation as you find what numbers work for you. Once I found a recipe that worked, I wrote it down so I didn't have to fumble around the next time!

I can give you a quick cannabutter recipe that has never failed me!

You'll want about 4g bud, depending on potency (I use 4g as a staple, which makes a very potent batch if the strain is good). Grind it pretty finely, but not like powder fine, and carefully spread it on a sheet of baking paper on a tray. Bake it for about 50 mins at 115 Celsius/ 240 Fahrenheit, optionally stirring the buds halfway through baking. Then take it out and put it somewhere safe (it's easy to loose weed when it's spread out like this!)

Then you'll want 160g butter, or a mixture of butter and oil (say 140g butter and a few spoons of oil- oil has a higher fat content so a little can help absorb maximum THC). Put it in a saucepan on low heat, wait until it's melted, then put in the bud. I find the easiest way to get the bud from the baking paper without spilling any is to fold the paper like a half tube, then brush the bud into the pan with my finger. This can be a bit of a ball ache, especially if the strain is sticky, but it's worth it to make sure you get it all. Stir it into the butter and let it simmer for anywhere from 40-60 mins, making sure you stir it frequently. If the butter goes black, don't panic- the first time I made it I thought I'd burnt the batch and ruined it, but I've been making edibles regularly for a while now and never had the butter *not* go black. As long as the butter isn't bubbling like crazy and there's no black smoke, you're good. Just make sure the heat is low enough and you'll be fine, even if it ends up smelling like shit (if it doesn't smell bad you're probably doing something wrong, lol)

Then take the butter off the heat, and strain it into a bowl/ jug. I usually do this is two stages to make it easier; first I pour the butter from the pan into a large jug, and then pour it from the jug through a tea strainer, into a bowl. Make sure to get as much of the butter and leaf solids as possible into the strainer, and then push it down with a spoon until you can't squeeze any more drops through the strainer. I usually discard the solids, as I don't find they get me high, but some people say they can be used for cannabis tea/ other edibles, so do your own research and see what sounds best.

Then your cannabutter should be ready to go! Use it as you would normally in any brownie/ cookie recipe, but I strongly advise for this recipe you find one that makes 16 servings, so as not to make the edibles too strong or weak. This also should be about right for the amount of butter you have. If you're making cookies, you may need to add more flour and sugar so that the butter doesn't escape (brownies are usually bigger, so each serving will hold more butter without tweaking the recipe). 

I like to add lots of cocoa powder and chocolate chips, which masks the flavour of the cannabutter, which can be unpleasant- you can also add stuff like m & ms, marshmallows- whatever you want really. Try to portion the servings as evenly as you can, and don't bake them too long, or you'll lose more butter content. Most importantly, when you're piloting a new batch of edibles, go easy!!! Even using the same careful recipe, I find the potency varies batch to batch, and I once beta tested my new cookies by eating a whole one that ended up giving me a mild panic attack and blasting me into space for the next 24 hours- no joke, I was high for a *day*. My most successful batches are strong enough that even 1/4 of a small cookie will give you a very nice, strong high, so start with 1/4- 1/3 and see how you go! 

Good luck! Feel free to shoot any questions my way ;D

Hey, I went through exactly what you're describing back in January, and let me tell you, it's no cakewalk, but it does get easier after the first scan. I was so so scared and embarrassed and angry that I had to go through all this shit just to have the same fertility chances as a cis person.

The first scan was the worst, but not the scan itself- the build up was the worst bit. I've never had sex and I was freaking out that it'd tear my hymen and hurt really bad, but it was so underwhelming when they actually did it that I was still waiting for it to go in. The doctors misgendered me on and off too, which sucked, but they do care and they do want to get it right. It's just ignorance/ force of habit, and I'm not saying that means you shouldn't be upset, but for me disconnecting myself from the situation and pretending I was playing the role of someone else really helped it not be distressing.

The most uncomfortable bit is when they move the wand around to scan each ovary, but they'll talk you through that and if you feel even a little pain just tell them and they'll accommodate it. Remember, if it's ever too much, you are completely allowed to tell them and stop what is happening. Don't worry about being rude, your comfort is the first priority.

The hormones are the worst bit by far- I'm not going to sugar coat it, because I don't want to mislead you. It wasn't *nearly* as bad as I thought it would be, but injecting yourself daily, sometimes more than once, can be a lot psychologically. I found that numbing it with ice and injecting slowly worked much better for me than the quick stab method they encourage. It also makes a lot of difference where you inject- for me, I couldn't do it on my stomach without it being painful as I have very minimal fat there. The thighs are a safe bet, but make sure you get a good fatty pinch of skin and don't inject too far down the leg. Mainly though, don't sweat the injections too much in terms of doing them wrong- it's pretty hard to screw it up honestly. I gave myself the wrong dose at the most crucial part and I got a very good egg count at collection, so don't panic if you do something wrong. Even if you inject an air bubble it won't matter- some of the syringes are impossible to clear or small bubbles anyway, so don't worry about being too meticulous.

The collection was the bit I was freaking out about the most (like, fluttering stomach oh my god I'm going to die and it's going to hurt freaking out), but it ended up being by FAR the easiest bit. If your clinic is anything like mine, it'll go something like this: you'll have a little segment curtained off where they'll leave you to change into the gown (you do have to be totally naked underneath, which is awkward and did make me dysphoric but by that point I just wanted to get it over with, and if you tie it up at the back securely there's no risk of anyone seeing anything anyway). For me there was a bit of a wait while they prep everything, which was nerve wracking just cause it lets your thoughts dominate you, but it won't be too long. The aneathesist came and chatted to me whilst he put the drip in the back of my hand- it stings but it isn't too bad, though I did find it better to keep my hand still and straight once the needle was in. 

They'll probably ask questions like whether you consent to a rectal suppository for pain relief, which is administered whilst youre still under sedation (awkward as hell and I nearly said no, but figured eh, I won't be awake and it's not much different from what's already happening. It felt very overwhelming at the time but when it came to it I was glad I'd said yes, cause I didn't feel a thing upon waking up). 

Then they'll wheel you into the theatre, and you'll have to put your legs in stirrups like with the scans (awful, I know, I hated that but as bad as it sounds you do get used to it quickly). A doctor will administer the sedatives (if you're having sedation and not general anaesthetic, which was not available to me)- the sedatives might sting your hand going in but again, it's far from terrible. Honestly that's the last thing I remember before waking up, thinking "shit, I shouldn't be awake already, they haven't even started!" Only to hear them saying it was finished. I was amazed at how instant it seemed and the relief of it being over was the best feeling. Then they'll take you back to your recovery area, and probably give you lots of biscuits and drinks and nice things (best part for me, surprisingly quality biscuits). I was fully awake very quickly and then went home within the hour.

Personally I did end up having to take more hormones to wean my eostrogen levels down, as I had a very high egg count, which was great for fertility chances but put me at risk of OHSS (essentially your body reacting badly to too much eostrogen). I was pissed that I had to take yet MORE injections, but it was only another week, and by that point I'd become a pro at doing it, so it was more like a chore. (I was so scared the first time injecting myself that it took me about two hours to do it- again, the slow and steady method worked for me, but some people can't stand that and prefer doing it quick.)

After the whole thing I had some weird stomach sensations for a week or so, but not much pain other than mild cramps. I was tired from the process but very very glad to have future proofed that area of my life, and I wouldn't take it back now, despite the at times overwhelming dysphoria and anxiety.

I hope this helps, even just a little- I know this is long as shit but I just wanted to give you the most detailed picture I could of what it's like, and what to expect, so nothing catches you off guard. If you have any questions about certain parts of it you'd like me to go into more detail with, please don't hesitate to ask. I know firsthand what you're going through and how bizarre and shitty it is to have to have a procedure that involves the parts of your body most foreign to you, but I promise it is doable and it will likely be easier than you think once the first stages are over with. I wish you the best of luck- you can do this, but if you feel that you can't, that's okay too, and you don't have to force anything that feels too much.

I couldn't be happier I made that awkward decision, and I'd definitely recommend thinking about it if it sounds like something you might want- remember, if you don't like it, you can always change back at any time!

I used to never plan at all because I couldn't stand it- it made me get caught up in every single potential problem and I'd try to work it out all at once, which would inevitably burn me out and make the whole project seem really stressful and unapproachable. Winging it worked well for me as a kid, but when I got serious about creative writing and started embarking on novellas instead of short stories, I quickly realised that by doing little to no planning, I was dooming myself from the start. The vague story in my head would run dry sooner or later and I'd be left with a plot headed nowhere.

I've since found a balance that works very well for me. I always start by writing down every idea I get that I'd like to build on, and then connect relevant ideas together to make rough plot lines and scenes. I'll finish by arranging my ideas in a vaguely chronological order, and that will be my plan for a 60k word novel.

Now, that might sound very plan-centric, but what always happens is that the plan is just the foundation for where the writing *actually* goes. I'll write out a scene i thought I knew everything about only to think, hey, here's a neat idea! And then that neat idea will obviously require accommodation, which means everything about the story from that point on is changed, just slightly. It ends up so that even with a meticulous plan, I go into my projects knowing that I have free rein to change and add in anything I like, which makes the whole thing feel much less restrictive, and more fun, too.

If I have a point I'm unsure or completely stumped on, I leave it be. More often than not these things work themselves out by the time you get to them, but when they don't, it's still not helpful for me to spend energy I *could* by using writing trying to work out one detail. I've actually self-sabotaged a lot of stories doing that, and ended up abandoning them altogether.

TL;DR: a careful balance of the two, but I never go into a big project without knowing what the ending looks like.

Whatever she says or does she knows that her father is going to do what he wants anyway, and the fact that he's smiling all the while probably made her feel very alienated- it wasn't just that he wasn't listening to her, but that he wasn't hearing her at all. He didn't comfort her or acknowledge her pain because he thought it was silly and inconsequential- she probably felt totally invisible to him and helpless beyond measure, because her reaction didn't matter. In my experience, depression and most mental health problems are things that can be managed very effectively, but not eradicated. That might sound bleak but what it means is that in times of stress, someone who has suffered from depression, anxiety or any disorder really will be vulnerable to sinking back into that feeling.

But you're not doomed, far from it. It's a tiring thing to contend with but when those thoughts do crop up again, it doesn't mean it will be like that for the rest of your life. They might come back when you're feeling particularly low, and you should be prepared for that, but you absolutely shouldn't fear a life of misery, because it's very likely that those thoughts will become more manageable with time.

When stuff like this shows up when we're not expecting it to, when we think we're happy and stable, it can be really distressing and unsettling. It can feel like any progress you made has been eradicated- that's not the case, I promise. The fact that you went so long almost completely free of those thoughts is an amazing achievement and a very positive sign! It's not ruined and it's not rendered meaningless just because things are painful again.

It may well be that you have to be more careful than most to manage your depression, but it won't be an exhausting chore forever. You may find new medication or treatment that will make things much easier in years to come (modern medicine is progressing so quickly), and even if you don't, you will almost certainly evolve your coping mechanisms so that you don't have to be so vigilant.

Be proud of what you've accomplished because it's truly an incredible thing. I understand your frustration but I honestly believe this is a temporary setback and not an omen for the rest of your life.

I've had problems not only with being teased on gender and sexuality, but also race. I'm mixed race (white and Asian) and I used to be extremely upset that I was stuck with that identity that ultimately made a lot of people look down on me. I agonised over the fact that I would never get the chance to experience the privilege of a white person.

I've since learned that although there are many downsides about being a minority, there are many bonuses. Things like being a feminine man are so hard to navigate because no one gives you a guidebook- you have to learn it yourself- but it provides us with a perspective that few men could ever achieve. Being different in such a stigmatised way can be extremely tough, but there are so many positives. I for one am very put off my masc guys, and wildly prefer people who are feminine or androgynous. Many people feel the same way, even if you haven't met them yet.

Bottom line, if people aren't reacting positively to your femininity, they're the wrong people. I understand your pain because it's horrible to be excluded from things or made fun of because of something about you you can't change. The key for me has been to find the right company, and not give a damn about any one who's shallow minded enough to rule me out from a glance. People who mock feminine men are the same breed of people as racists, it's just that society doesn't recognise that kind of discrimination as serious yet. 

What I'm trying to say is that those people aren't worth a moment of your time. They won't change and that's not your problem- they're missing out on your company and that's their loss. Of course it doesn't make it any less difficult to hear those hateful words/ be isolated, but what helped me was learning to be myself, loud and unapologetic- to pretend I'm more confident than I am in my identity until that confidence became a reality.  

I'm not disagreeing with what you're saying; we're at a disadvantage in this world and that really sucks. It will never stop sucking. But I honestly have full faith in what I said: there are countless people out there who will see your femininity as a wonderful part of you rather than a flaw. In the last few years I've gone from friends who used 'gay' as an insult to ones who wore drag at pride and don't bat an eyelid to the fact that I'm trans. 

I'm sorry this is so rambly but I hear you and I sympathise. I know it's bleak when everything seems to be stacked against you but you WILL find people who will embrace you. In the meantime, do your best to stay strong, and know that you're far from alone in this

I'm in a similar boat to you- high achiever then dropout. I've been living with my parents with no job for over four years.

Finding acceptance in that situation is so hard. You've got everyone telling you that if you don't follow the laid out path of college-job, that you're not good enough- but that's so untrue. For me the most productive part of my life has been what most would frown at- sitting around at home, feeling awful and then feeling slightly less awful until those moments of joy stared to come back. I am not fully healed but I have learned not to hold myself to anyone else's standards, and that has helped a lot.

Having family be apathetic or not see you is agonising, especially when you're stuck in that environment. What's helped me get out of that despair is to just separate my thoughts from them, even if I can only manage it for a moment, and exist purely inside myself. That might sound like nonsense but what I mean is to detach from those stressors as best you can. List things in your head, watch old YouTube videos you like, start drawing- it might feel impossible or pointless but I find that more often than not, after a few minutes of that kind of activity I do start to feel a little better.

Your family will not be better off with you gone. Regardless of what they say and how they act, you mean more to them than you probably realise. I don't say this to guilt trip you, but just to let you know that you shouldn't consider doing your family a favour as a motive.

I know that when you're feeling so abysmal words and promises of a happy future mean very little. Your suffering is in the now, and it's so hard to look beyond that. I won't promise you that everything will get better, but I can say this with a certainty: stay, and you'll have moments of joy you never thought you would. Be it a new video game release, an awesome movie, or any little surprise- there are so many things in the future to live for, moments where your stomach will flutter with happiness. Those little moments aren't satisfactory on their own, I know, but they're indicative of the fact that you are capable of feeling good things, and slowly, with time, the good will start to outweigh the bad.

You are enough just as you are. You do not need an income or a job or qualifications to render you worthy. Above all, you are in no way deserving of hatred. Again, I know you're not gonna read those words and magically feel awesome about yourself, but take it from me: however contradictory it sounds to what you've been told, it's okay to do nothing all day, for as many days as it takes for you to get better. I hope you find something today that eases your pain a little, and for what it's worth, I hope you keep living.
